title: Industry sponsorship and research outcome
authors: Lundh A, Lexchin J, Mintzes B, Schroll JB, Bero L
funder: Internal sources: Center for Evidence-Based Medicine, Odense; The Nordic Cochrane Centre, Copenhagen (no financial support); University of Sydney; York University (author salaries). External sources: no sources of support supplied.
authorConflicts: Lundh, Lexchin and Bero authored previous reviews and some included studies. Lexchin received payment from non-profit entities and from a for-profit company for a panel on drug coverage in Canada. Mintzes was retained as an expert witness for plaintiffs in Canadian class actions on hormone replacement therapy and testosterone.
result: 75 papers. Industry-sponsored drug and device studies more often had favourable efficacy results (RR 1.27, 95% CI 1.17 to 1.37; 25 papers, 2923 studies; 638 versus 502 per 1000) and favourable conclusions (RR 1.34, 1.19 to 1.51; 29 papers, 4583 studies; 863 versus 644 per 1000). Risk of bias did not differ for sequence generation, allocation concealment, follow-up or selective outcome reporting; industry studies more often had low risk of bias from blinding (RR 1.25, 1.05 to 1.50) and showed less agreement between results and conclusions (RR 0.83, 0.70 to 0.98).
